intro: Long ago, children in England and America played bat-and-ball games on any open ground. A book from 1744 has a rhyme called "Base-Ball." A Massachusetts town banned the game near its meeting house in 1791. Every town had its own way to play, with bases wherever players put them.

Then clubs began to write the game down. The Knickerbocker club of New York adopted written rules in 1845. Clubs set the bases 90 feet apart in 1857. Writers like Henry Chadwick printed box scores, and leagues kept standings. Chicago and Illinois became part of this story, from the White Stockings of 1876 to the Rockford Peaches.

In this unit, you will learn how the baseball diamond got its measured lines. You will be able to name the papers that set its rules. You will tell a legend apart from a record. You will also see who was left out of the early books, and when doors opened.
bigQuestion: How did measured lines and written records turn many backyard games into one shared game of baseball?

timeline.t: A London children's book prints a rhyme called "Base-Ball"
Pittsfield, Massachusetts, bans ball games near its meeting house
The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club adopts 20 written rules
A convention of clubs sets bases 90 feet apart and games at nine innings
Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player, edited by Henry Chadwick, goes on sale
The National League forms; Chicago wins its first pennant
The pitcher's plate is set 60 feet 6 inches from home plate
Illinois high schools form the IHSA; home plate gets five sides
The Mills Commission report repeats the Doubleday legend
Rube Foster helps found the Negro National League
Little League begins; the Hall of Fame opens in Cooperstown
The All-American Girls Professional Baseball League begins

words.d: an empty lot used for pick-up games with no official field
a rule made by a town or club, like Pittsfield's 1791 ban on ball games
the 20 rules adopted by a New York club on September 23, 1845
a meeting where groups decide things together, like the 1857 meeting that set 90 feet
a story people repeat that cannot be proved, like the Doubleday story
papers, objects or records that show something really happened
the rubber slab 60 feet 6 inches from home plate since 1893
a printed table of each player's numbers from one game
a table of every team's wins and losses
a drawing that shows a layout from above, like the field in the rule book
the Illinois High School Association, formed in 1900
an unfair barrier that kept Black players out of white clubs and leagues

choices: base-ball was a children's game in England by 1744
test.why: Its "Base-Ball" rhyme shows children played the game in 1744.

test.q: Which town passed a bylaw naming baseball in 1791?
test.why: Pittsfield banned ball games near its new meeting house in 1791.

test.q: How did the Knickerbocker Rules of 1845 measure the bases?
test.why: The 1845 rules set the bases 42 paces apart from home to second.

choices: home plate would have five sides
the pitcher would stand 60 feet 6 inches away
bases would be 90 feet apart and games nine innings
test.why: The 1857 convention set 90 feet and nine innings.

test.q: Which statement is a legend, not a documented fact?
choices: Doubleday invented baseball at Cooperstown in 1839
test.why: The Doubleday story came from one letter and a 1907 report; historians call it a legend.

test.q: Who helped create the box score?
test.why: Henry Chadwick, a New York writer, helped shape the box score.

test.q: Why did the pitcher move back in 1893?
choices: to give batters a fairer chance
to fit the new home plate
test.why: Pitchers had grown stronger, so the league moved the plate to 60 feet 6 inches.

test.q: Which Chicago club won the first National League pennant?
test.why: Chicago's White Stockings won in 1876 with 52 wins and 14 losses.
Standings list wins and losses so a league can pick a champion.

test.q: IHSA records list track champions from 1893. Why is that surprising?
choices: the IHSA was not formed until 1900
Illinois was not a state in 1893
the IHSA does not keep track records
test.why: The IHSA formed in 1900 but kept earlier written results.

test.q: What does the rule book diagram show?
choices: the field seen from above with its distances
test.why: The Layout of the Field diagram shows the measured field.

test.q: What happened to the Pythian Base Ball Club in 1867?
choices: the national association refused to admit it
test.why: The association turned away the Black Pythian club, an early sign of the color line.
Carl Stotz started Little League in Williamsport, Pennsylvania.

test.q: Which team played in the women's professional league from 1943 to 1954?
test.why: The Rockford Peaches of Illinois played every season of the league.

test.q: What makes the Wrigley Field scoreboard different from a scorebook?
choices: the whole crowd can read it
it is kept by the umpire
test.why: The 1937 scoreboard shows the score to everyone in the park.

write.prompt: Who deserves credit for baseball's shape: one inventor, or many people over time? Argue your answer using two or three dated records from this unit, such as the 1744 Pocket-Book, the 1791 Pittsfield bylaw, the 1845 Knickerbocker Rules, the 1857 convention or the 1907 Mills Commission report.
tips: Name each record and give its year.
Say clearly which story is a legend and which is a record.
Tell who made each rule: a town, a club, a convention or a league.
Use unit words such as bylaw, convention, evidence and legend.
End with one sentence that answers the question in your own words.
